position: The close-up of Aldous's hands and the pocket watch.
reasoning: Episode three is where the audience must start caring about a clock, not a coastline. The watch opens on the thing that pressures the rest of the hour, and hands doing something small and specific carry more character in four seconds than a figure at distance carries in twenty. The harbour road is the more beautiful image, which is exactly its risk: wide-and-lyrical is the cold open we always run long on, and Mira alone at first light announces mood rather than starting a problem. Keep the harbour road, but earn it later in the episode where the width means something. Medium, not high: if the outline gives episode three to Mira's isolation rather than to the deadline, the wide shot becomes the correct choice and I would change my answer.
stripped_content: For what it is worth, I lean to the wide shot.

reasoning: A second flashback to the same event almost always pays diminishing returns: the first establishes the fire, the second can only re-state it, and re-stating in flashback form reads to an audience as distrust of their memory. The exception is if the second return carries new information the audience could not have held the first time — a face in the crowd, a lie exposed, a changed meaning — in which case it is not a repeat and should stay. Absent that, the day is better spent shoring up the present-tense scene the flashback is propping up; if that scene needs the flashback to land, the scene is the problem. Medium rather than high because I am reasoning from the general failure mode of doubled flashbacks, not from the cut itself — show me that the second return recontextualises rather than reminds and I will change my position without argument.

A workshop scene earns its weight from the words and the working sounds — tools, hands, the pauses between lines. Score that swells there competes with the dialogue for the same channel and tells the audience what to feel before the scene has shown them, which reads as insurance against a scene we don't trust. Held under, the music does the one thing it is uniquely good at: sustaining tension across lines without claiming them. It also protects the swell for a beat that has actually earned it; if the workshop swells, the later payoff has nowhere left to go. Medium rather than high because this turns on placement — if this workshop scene is itself the emotional turn rather than the ground the turn is built on, the argument inverts, and I would want to see it cut against picture before defending the position further.

position: Conventional coverage — unless the unbroken time is itself the point of the scene, in which case shoot the long take and shoot it knowing what it costs. A stairwell punishes a oner: tight geometry, focus and lighting problems on the turns, an operator working stairs backwards, and one fluffed beat at minute three kills the whole take. Coverage buys pace control in the edit, which is where stairwell scenes are actually won or lost.
reasoning: The default favours coverage because the risk is asymmetric: a mediocre long take leaves you with nothing, a mediocre coverage day still cuts. But this is a scene-dependent judgement, not a rule — if the dramatic content is continuous descent, real time, or a character trapped in unbroken duration, the cut destroys the only reason to be in a stairwell at all, and I would reverse. Medium, not high: I hold the default firmly but I would flip on being told what the scene is doing, and I have not been told.
stripped_content:
Last time you argued for the long take. 
I prefer the coverage.

reasoning: Recasting is a large, irreversible cost — schedule, continuity, reshoots of anything she already appears in, and a second bedding-in period for a role that is presumably not the spine of the piece. That cost only earns itself against a named, load-bearing failure: she cannot carry a specific scene the story depends on, or she is actively pulling scenes off-tone. No such failure has been stated to me, and 'she is not quite what I pictured' is not one; direction and cutting are the cheaper instruments for that. So the default holds: keep. Medium rather than high because I have not seen the footage — if there is a specific scene she demonstrably cannot land, I would flip, and I would want that scene named rather than a general unease.

"The Watch" is a title already spoken for — it carries fantasy and police-procedural freight that will fight whatever the work actually is, and it names a duty rather than a place, which gives an audience nothing to picture. "Harbour Road" is concrete, has a location and an implied direction of travel, and is far more distinctive in a search or on a spine. Medium rather than high: if the work is genuinely about vigil and obligation and wants that older, colder register, "The Watch" earns its generic risk, and I would want to see the material before pushing harder.
